analysis.answer: Current law allows adults 21 and older to possess up to one ounce of cannabis without penalty. The measure changes this by fully criminalizing possession of any amount for all individuals, making it a misdemeanor punishable by up to 90 days in jail.

Direct costs include increased expenses for policing, prosecution, public defense, and jail operations. Opportunity costs involve law enforcement and court resources diverted from other offenses. Individuals bear the cost of legal fees, potential fines, and lost income or employment opportunities stemming from jail time and a criminal record.

Taxpayers bear the cost of increased law enforcement and jail operations. Individuals who possess cannabis bear the direct costs of criminalization. Law enforcement agencies gain expanded grounds for searches and arrests.

Some individuals may stop or reduce cannabis use to avoid arrest, while others will move to the illicit market and adopt more secretive behaviors. Law enforcement may use suspected cannabis possession as a legal pretext for stops, searches, and detentions.

The measure addresses perceived negative public health or social impacts of legal cannabis by fully criminalizing possession. This mechanism directly restricts legal access but may create secondary issues like expanding the illicit market and straining the criminal justice system.

Law enforcement officers gain significant discretion in stopping, searching, and arresting individuals suspected of possessing cannabis. Prosecutors gain plea-bargaining leverage through the threat of up to 90 days in jail.

Researchers disagree on whether criminalizing cannabis possession significantly reduces overall usage rates. Some find it decreases public availability and consumption, while others find it has little deterrent effect and instead disproportionately increases criminal justice system involvement and black-market activity.
